## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Report the ceiling as a tiered bracket rather than a single number (chain C1, chain C3): the absolute Carnot ceiling is **60.8–62.6%** (dry vs. wet cooling); the naive Curzon–Ahlborn figure often quoted for this purpose (**37.4–38.9%**) is not a valid ceiling here and is retained only as an illustrative reference (chain C2); the physically honest ceiling for a real steam-Rankine architecture at these boundary temperatures is **53–57%** (chain C3). Current best-demonstrated practice sits at **≈41–43% gross / ≈36–40% net** (chain C4), leaving a total Carnot-to-net gap of roughly **21–25 percentage points**, decomposed as: **≈6–8 points** structurally irreducible for any steam-Rankine engine at these temperatures (chain C4, Segment 1); **≈12–14 points** from real finite-rate irreversibility within the Rankine architecture (chain C4, Segment 2), of which roughly **2–5 points** are realistically engineering-recoverable near-term at a fixed 565°C salt temperature and roughly **7–10 points** are technically closeable but economically stuck under current capital-cost economics; and **≈4 points** of plant-level parasitic losses recoverable through balance-of-plant optimization (chain C4, Segment 3).

**Key insight:** The single biggest correction to the naive "how far below Carnot are we" framing is not a Curzon–Ahlborn finite-power correction at all — it is the simple structural fact that a steam Rankine cycle cannot receive heat isothermally at the peak salt temperature (GT8). Roughly a third of the raw Carnot-to-practice gap (chain C3's Segment 1, ≈6–8 of ≈21–25 points) is baked into the Rankine cycle's own architecture before any turbine or heat-exchanger engineering enters the picture at all.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Pursuing the economically-stuck ≈7–10 point band of Segment 2 trades capital cost and CSP-specific cycling-fatigue risk against efficiency gain, and some industry/national-lab effort is instead directed at abandoning the Rankine architecture altogether (supercritical-CO₂ Brayton topping) rather than closing this gap (chain C5). Dry cooling, adopted for water-scarce siting (as at Noor III, GT4), forfeits roughly 1.5–2 Carnot-equivalent points relative to wet cooling by deliberate design choice, not technology immaturity (chains C1, C5).

The full analysis is done. Here's the summary:

## The ceiling(s)

There isn't one honest "ceiling" — there are three, and conflating them is the main way this question gets misreported:

| Tier | Value | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| **Absolute Carnot** | 60.8–62.6% | Pure 2nd-law bound between 565°C salt (838 K) and ambient condenser (40°C wet / 55°C dry). Zero-power, reversible, architecture-agnostic. |
| **Naive Curzon-Ahlborn** | 37.4–38.9% | The commonly-cited "finite-power" correction (η=1−√(Tc/Th)). **Not actually a valid ceiling here** — real plants already beat it. It's derived for one narrow symmetric two-reservoir model that doesn't match a multi-stage regenerative Rankine cycle, so it's discarded as the bound (kept only as a reference curiosity). |
| **Reversible regenerative-Rankine ceiling** ("Tier C") | 53–57% | The physically honest ceiling for *this specific architecture*. A Rankine cycle can't add heat isothermally at 565°C — it ramps through economizer→evaporation→superheat (~290°C to ~540°C), so even an ideal version of this cycle tops out at Carnot evaluated at the *mean* temperature of heat addition (~690–730 K), not peak temperature. |

**Key insight:** ~6–8 of the ~21–25 point gap between Carnot and current practice is baked into the Rankine cycle's own shape — not a shortfall of engineering. No amount of turbine/heat-exchanger polish closes that segment; only a different cycle architecture (isothermal topping cycle, alternative working fluid, or a Brayton/sCO2 topping combined cycle) would.

## Current practice vs. the gap

Best-demonstrated real plants run **~41–43% gross / ~36–40% net** at 565°C hot salt. Total gap to Carnot ≈ 21–25 points, decomposed as:

- **~6–8 pts** — structural (non-isothermal heat addition) — **irreducible for any steam-Rankine engine**, full stop
- **~12–14 pts** — real finite-rate irreversibility (salt/steam pinch, turbine/pump isentropic losses, finite feedwater-heater stages, condenser approach) — of this, only **~2–5 pts** are realistically engineering-recoverable near-term (supercritical steam, better matching to 565°C), and **~7–10 pts** are technically closeable but **economically stuck** given current capital costs and CSP's daily-cycling fatigue burden on thick-walled components
- **~4 pts** — plant-level parasitics (pumps, cooling fans, freeze protection) — recoverable through balance-of-plant work, largely independent of the core cycle

## Honest confidence caveat

The agent rates this **LOW confidence overall** — not because the physics is shaky (Carnot and the regenerative-Rankine identity are solid derivations), but because the two most load-bearing real-world numbers (current best-demonstrated 41–43% gross efficiency, and the net-efficiency parasitic deduction) came from web-search summaries of an OSTI report and general engineering judgment — a direct PDF fetch and a ScienceDirect page both failed to open in the session, so those figures weren't confirmed at primary source. The physics/architecture conclusions (Tiers 1 and "Tier C", and the structural-gap finding) are more solid than the exact recoverable/stuck split inside the middle segment.
